notes: Food for home consumption is exempt, bakery goods and dietary supplements included. Candy, soft drinks and food from vending machines are taxed at 7%, which is not counted here; prepared food is taxed at 7% (8% at restaurants and other eating places).

Alcohol bought in stores: beer bought in stores is taxed at 7%, but wine and spirits sold by liquor stores have been exempt since December 1, 2013 (made permanent in 2015). Counted here at 7% on beer's share of liquor stores' alcohol sales in 2024, 31.2% (wine and spirits 68.8%), from the Division of Taxation's report on stores' 2024 returns, 2.18% in all. The same report gives $161.8 million of net taxable sales of alcoholic beverages without reconciling it with beer's $128.4 million; counted on that figure, the rate would be 2.75%, so the 2.18% used here is the lower of the two. Stores that hadn't filed by the report's cutoff made less than 14.63% of sales. Drinks served at restaurants and bars pay 8% (the sales tax and the 1% local meals and beverage tax), counted in the rate for drinks served. Excise taxes of $3.30 a barrel of beer, $1.40 a gallon of still wine and $5.40 a gallon of spirits are left out here.

Cigarettes and other tobacco are taxed at 7%, on top of excise taxes left out here: $4.50 a pack of 20 cigarettes (since September 1, 2024; the 2026 session changed no tobacco rate), 80% of the wholesale cost of other tobacco products (cigars capped at 50 cents each; nicotine pouches included since October 1, 2025), $1.00 an ounce of snuff, and 50 cents a milliliter of e-liquid in closed vaping products (10% of wholesale cost on other vaping products) since January 1, 2025.
Household supplies: diapers are taxed at 7%; Rhode Island's list of exemptions has none for them.
Personal care products: menstrual products (tampons, pads, panty liners, menstrual cups) have been exempt since October 1, 2019, which is not taken out here.
Barber and beauty services aren't taxed.

Clothing and footwear are exempt up to $250 an item. Jewelry and watches, clothing accessories under the law, are taxed at 7% and counted on their share of US sales of clothing, shoes and jewelry (13%, 2022 Economic Census), 0.91% of what is spent on clothing, shoes and jewelry; the category's rate also takes in laundry and dry cleaning, at their own rate. Also taxed but not counted, since no official figure gives their share: the part of an item's price over $250, other accessories such as handbags, and sports or protective clothing. Rhode Island has no sales tax holiday.
Laundry and dry cleaning aren't taxed.
Gasoline is exempt from sales tax and pays the motor fuel tax instead, left out here: 40 cents a gallon since July 1, 2025 (was 37 cents), adjusted for inflation every two years from July 1, 2027.
Repair labor billed separately isn't taxed; parts are.

Rhode Island has no local sales taxes, and no city or town sales, meals or hotel tax of its own was found; the 1% local meals and beverage tax and the local hotel tax are set by the state for every city and town. Providence's tourism improvement district charges hotels of 50 or more rooms 2% of room revenue (City Council, December 15, 2022; see Providence's page on this site).

Hotel and other stays of 30 days or less pay 14% in all since January 1, 2026 (the 7% sales tax, the 5% state hotel tax or, for a whole house or condominium, the new 5% whole-home short-term rental tax, and the local hotel tax, raised from 1% to 2%); none of these is counted here.
The 2026 legislative session changed no sales, meals, hotel, alcohol or cigarette tax rate (Division of Taxation, 2026 Summary of Legislative Changes).

Rhode Island taxes only the services its law lists (taxi, limousine and ride-hailing trips, charter buses, pet care, hotel room resellers, investigation and guard services and, since October 1, 2025, parking of less than a month); haircuts, laundry and dry cleaning and car repair labor are not among them.
gaps: Rhode Island has no local sales taxes; the 7% state rate applies everywhere. Restaurant meals and drinks also pay the statewide 1% local meals and beverage tax (8% in all), counted here; hotel and other short-term stays pay 14% since January 1, 2026 (7% sales tax, 5% state hotel or whole-home rental tax and a 2% local hotel tax), not counted.

programs: Rhode Island has no statewide map of its programs, and none of its cities' program layers is loaded here. Named, not mapped: Providence's Downtown Improvement District and its tourism improvement district, the I-195 Redevelopment District, and Pawtucket's downtown redevelopment area (Tidewater Landing). Main Street Rhode Island, a three-year pilot run by Grow Smart RI under a 2025 joint resolution, works with 11 local teams in 10 communities, as Grow Smart RI reported in testimony to the General Assembly; the list hasn't been published. Enterprise zones are left out: no new credits have been allowed since July 1, 2015 (R.I. Gen. Laws 42-64.3-6). The Distressed Communities Relief Fund goes in fiscal 2027 to Central Falls, Coventry, East Providence, North Providence, Pawtucket, Providence, West Warwick and Woonsocket (House Fiscal Advisory Staff, State Aid to Local Governments, FY 2027).

warn.text: Providence draws many visitors (its downtown and convention center, WaterFire and its colleges), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy over the city as a whole: its seasonal homes (0.2%) and its 45 lodging places (0.2 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs, though one of its 42 census tracts is flagged on its own. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

programs: Providence's Downtown Improvement District, a special assessment district for downtown property owners, isn't mapped (no public boundary layer was found).

Providence's tourism improvement district, approved by the City Council on December 15, 2022, assesses hotels of 50 or more rooms in the district 2% of their room revenue (R.I. Gen. Laws 45-59.1); no official record found says whether hotels add it to guests' bills, and it isn't counted (lodging isn't counted on this site in any case).
The state's I-195 Redevelopment District (R.I. Gen. Laws 42-64.14), the land freed by moving Interstate 195, isn't mapped.
Providence receives the state's Distressed Communities Relief Fund in fiscal 2027.

warn.text: Newport East draws many visitors (Middletown's beaches and the hotels on the way into Newport), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy over the community as a whole: its seasonal homes (7.6%) and its 25 lodging places (1.6 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs, though 2 of its 4 census tracts are flagged on their own. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

The town of Middletown draws many visitors (Second and Third Beaches, Sachuest Point and the hotels on the way into Newport), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy over the town as a whole: its seasonal homes (7.0%) and its 25 lodging places (1.5 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs, though 2 of its 5 census tracts are flagged on their own. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

The Westerly Census place (the village; the town of Westerly around it is flagged as a visitor economy) draws many visitors (its downtown and Wilcox Park, near the beaches of Misquamicut and Watch Hill), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy over the place as a whole: its seasonal homes (2.9%) and its 4 lodging places (0.2 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs. The census tract it shares with Bradford, which holds 64 of Westerly's 411 census blocks and is left out of this page because Westerly is under half of it, has 12.6% of its homes seasonal, over the flag's cutoff. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Warwick draws visitors (the hotels by Rhode Island T. F. Green International Airport and Warwick Mall), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy over the city as a whole: its seasonal homes (0.4%) and its 27 lodging places (0.3 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Wakefield-Peace Dale draws visitors (the South County beaches and the University of Rhode Island nearby), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy over the community as a whole: its seasonal homes (4.1%) and its 6 lodging places (0.6 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Kingston's page is built from the census tract of the University of Rhode Island's campus, with 5,762 residents but only 182 homes. Its flag as a visitor economy rests on the tract's 14 lodging places (2.4 per 1,000 residents), 11 of them listed only as general lodging, so read that flag with care.

Bradford's page is built from a census tract in the town of Westerly: of its 155 census blocks, 36 are in Bradford, 64 in the Westerly Census place (the village) and 55 in neither. The tract's flag as a visitor economy rests on its seasonal homes (310 of 2,462, 12.6%, with 4 lodging places), which the figures here don't place within the tract, so they may lie mostly outside Bradford; read that flag with care.

Melville's page is built from one census tract, shared with Newport East, which holds 20 of Melville's 57 census blocks; the tract holding most of the rest, in Portsmouth (29 blocks), and one more (8 blocks) are left out because Melville is under half of each, so the figures here describe only part of Melville. None of the three tracts is flagged as a visitor economy.

programs: Pawtucket's downtown redevelopment area, including Tidewater Landing, is financed by state and city tax increment under R.I. Gen. Laws 45-33.4; it isn't mapped.
